In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
our sources are a mixture of absorbed AGN, unobscured AGN and Compton-thick objects.
XMM-Newton has allowed us to probe the faintest and deepest X-ray sky ever, and has shown that there is still a lot to be done.
our data do not show evidence for a population of intrinsically harder X-ray sources, but rather for a population of absorbed X-ray sources.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the X-ray spectra of the faintest X-ray sources detected in deep X-ray surveys do not show significant differences with respect to the brightest sources.
the average spectral properties of our sources are consistent with those expected from a population of absorbed AGN with an underlying intrinsic power law shape.
the XMM-Newton data for this field are in good agreement with the results obtained from Chandra and XMM-Newton for the other deep X-ray surveys.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the average X-ray spectral shape of the faint AGN population does not differ from that of the bright AGN population, but the fraction of absorbed AGN increases at faint fluxes.
the X-ray spectral properties of AGN are not a strong function of X-ray flux, but rather depend on their optical spectral class (i.e. type).
the average spectral slope of faint AGN is not harder than the average spectral slope at brighter fluxes, and that the average intrinsic absorbing column density does not depend on X-rays flux.
